## Objectif
Entraîner Louis OS à transformer ses capacités en revenus réels, hors charbon, en explorant plusieurs métiers et plateformes légales puis en comparant leur potentiel économique sur des preuves vérifiables.

## Principe
Chaque domaine est traité comme une expérience courte avec hypothèse, action réelle, preuve, métriques et décision continuer / pivoter / arrêter. Ne jamais confondre recherche, volume d'activité ou nombre de messages avec monétisation.

- missions ponctuelles et tests utilisateurs ;
- concours, bounties non techniques et petites prestations numériques ;
- vente de livrables réutilisables.

### Vague 2

buildPlan.summary: Implementation Specification for Entraînement ATLAS — test réel de monétisation multi-domaines
buildPlan.architectureNotes:
# Entraînement ATLAS – Technical Build & Implementation Plan  
**Project**: “Entraînement ATLAS — test réel de monétisation multi-domaines”  
**Goal**: Train Louis OS into a revenue‑generating engine across multiple legal platforms.  
**Stack** (Vague 2): Next.js 14 (App Router), Tailwind CSS, TypeScript, Node.js, Supabase, Redis, Docker, Vercel.  

> **Delivery format** – 3 sections  
> 1. Executive Architecture Summary  
> 2. Threat Model & Security Boundaries  
> 3. Phased Implementation Roadmap (3 milestones + tasks)  

---

## 1. Executive Architecture Summary

| Layer | Purpose | Key Components | Deployment |
|-------|---------|----------------|------------|
| **Client** | User‑facing portal for experiments & dashboards | Next.js 14 (SSR + Edge) + Tailwind + TS | Vercel (edge & serverless) |
| **API Gateway** | Single entry point, routing, rate‑limiting, auth enforcement | Vercel Edge Functions + Cloudflare Tunnel (optional) | Vercel |
| **Micro‑services** | Domain‑specific logic (search, writing, translation, lead‑qualification, etc.) | Node.js 20 + NestJS/Express, TypeScript | Docker + Vercel Serverless Functions or a lightweight Kubernetes cluster (if >10 services) |
| **Data Layer** | Persistent storage & authentication | Supabase (PostgreSQL + Auth + Storage) | Supabase Cloud (managed) |
| **Cache** | Low‑latency look‑ups, rate‑limit counters | Redis (managed, e.g., Redis Cloud or self‑hosted on Vercel) | Docker / managed |
| **Observability** | Logging, tracing, metrics | OpenTelemetry (Node), Grafana Loki + Prometheus, Sentry | Docker + Vercel |
| **CI/CD** | Secure, reproducible builds & deployments | GitHub Actions + Docker Hub, Vercel Deployments | GitHub → Vercel |
| **Security & Governance** | Zero‑trust, least‑privilege, data‑protection | OIDC (Supabase Auth), JWT, CSP, HSTS, OWASP ASVS, Vault for secrets | Supabase + HashiCorp Vault (self‑hosted or managed) |

**Key design principles**

1. **Zero‑trust** – every request is authenticated & authorized; network segmentation is enforced via service‑to‑service tokens.
2. **Least privilege** – each micro‑service only has the database schema and API endpoints it needs.
3. **Defense‑in‑depth** – layered security: network isolation, runtime hardening, input validation, rate‑limiting, WAF.
4. **Performance‑first** – edge caching, CDN, Redis, async job queue, lazy loading of heavy modules.
5. **Observability & auditability** – structured logs, distributed tracing, audit logs for all data changes.
6. **Compliance** – GDPR‑ready (Supabase handles PII), PCI‑ready if needed for payment flows.

---

## 2. Threat Model & Security Boundaries

| Threat Actor | Asset at Risk | Attack Vectors | Mitigations |
|--------------|---------------|----------------|-------------|
| **External attackers** | API, data, user accounts | SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, SSRF, brute‑force, DDoS | Prepared statements, CSP, CSRF tokens, input sanitization, rate‑limit, WAF, Cloudflare protection |
| **Insider (dev, ops)** | Secrets, code, config | Mis‑configuration, privilege escalation | Vault + role‑based secrets, GitHub secrets, GitHub Actions audit, minimal Docker privileges |
| **Malicious users** | Service logic, revenue flows | Abuse of micro‑services, request flooding | JWT scopes, per‑service rate‑limits, quotas, audit logs |
| **Supply‑chain** | Dependencies | Compromised npm packages | Dependabot, Snyk, lockfiles, npm audit, reproducible builds |
| **Data exfiltration** | PII, business data | API leaks, mis‑configured storage | Encryption at rest (Supabase), TLS everywhere, access logs, S3 bucket policies |
| **Denial‑of‑Service** | Availability | Traffic spikes, resource exhaustion | Vercel Edge functions auto‑scale, Redis throttling, Cloudflare CDN, graceful degradation |
| **Code‑injection via user‑content** | Rendering engine | Malicious HTML, script injection | Sanitization libraries, server‑side rendering with safe defaults |

### Security Boundaries

1. **User Boundary** – Authenticated via Supabase OIDC, JWT signed with RS256, scopes per role (`user`, `admin`, `service`).
2. **Service Boundary** – Each micro‑service exposes only its public API; internal APIs are protected by mutual TLS (or mTLS‑style tokens).
3. **Data Boundary** – Database schemas are separated by role; only micro‑services with relevant roles can query tables.
4. **Network Boundary** – All services communicate over a private VPC (if using a Kubernetes cluster) or via Vercel’s internal routing. No inbound ports exposed except the API Gateway.
5. **Secrets Boundary** – Secrets stored in Vault, injected into containers at runtime; never committed to repo.

---

## 3. Phased Implementation Roadmap

### **Milestone 1 – Foundation (Weeks 1‑4)**  
**Goal**: Establish core infrastructure, security baseline, and a reusable monorepo skeleton.

| Task | Owner | Deliverables | Notes |
|------|-------|--------------|-------|
| **1.1** – Set up GitHub monorepo (packages: `frontend`, `api`, `infra`) | DevOps | GitHub repo with CI templates | Use `pnpm` workspaces |
| **1.2** – Create Vercel project and link repo | DevOps | Vercel dashboard with preview & prod branches | |
| **1.3** – Spin up Supabase instance (auth + Postgres) | DevOps | Supabase project, database schema templates | Enable row‑level security |
| **1.4** – Deploy Redis (managed) | DevOps | Redis endpoint, TLS enabled | |
| **1.5** – Configure Vault (self‑hosted on a dedicated container) | Security | Vault server, secrets for DB credentials, API keys | Use sealed/unseal automation |
| **1.6** – Build CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions) | DevOps | Build/test/deploy workflows for `frontend`, `api` | Enforce code‑review gates |
| **1.7** – Implement basic OIDC + JWT auth in Next.js | Frontend | Login flow, token storage in HTTP‑Only cookie | CSP & HSTS headers |
| **1.8** – Create “Hello World” micro‑service (health‑check) | Backend | Node + Express, Dockerfile, API Gateway route | |
| **1.9** – Set up observability stack (OpenTelemetry, Loki, Prometheus) | DevOps | Dashboards, alerts | |
| **1.10** – Security hardening checklist (OWASP ASVS v4) | Security | Checklist, audit report | |

**Milestone Outcome**  
- Fully functional, zero‑trust dev environment.  
- All services can authenticate, log, and trace.  
- Secrets are centrally managed.  

---

### **Milestone 2 – Rapid‑Revenue Micro‑services (Weeks 5‑10)**  
**Goal**: Deploy first batch of micro‑services (search, writing, translation, lead‑qualification) and expose a simple marketplace UI.

| Task | Owner | Deliverables | Notes |
|------|-------|--------------|-------|
| **2.1** – Define data schemas for each domain | Data Engineer | Supabase tables, RLS policies | |
| **

problems.title: Bug: Newly added tasks do not appear on the Kanban board
problems.body:
When users add a new task through the form, the task is not appearing in any of the Kanban columns on the website. This prevents users from seeing their newly created tasks, including all their details. The task creation process itself might be succeeding, but the update or rendering logic for the board is not picking up the new task.

Steps to reproduce:
1. Navigate to the Kanban board.
2. Fill out the form to add a new task.
3. Submit the form.
Expected behavior: The new task should appear in the appropriate column on the board.
Actual behavior: The new task does not appear.
problems.author: BrianTruong23

problems.title: Server Actions missing CSRF token validation when invoked via raw fetch()
problems.body: When invoking Next.js App Router server actions via client fetch requests with specific headers, anti-CSRF token verification is bypassed if the Origin header is forged or missing in specific reverse proxy configurations. Developers building multi-tenant SaaS applications need an edge-level middleware guard to strictly enforce request authenticity.
problems.author: sec-researcher-42

problems.title: Ask HN: Why is local vector search in microservices still so painful?
problems.body: We are running hundreds of ephemeral container workers that need to do small KNN lookups (5k-10k items) for semantic deduplication. Cloud vector databases add 80-150ms round-trip latency and cost hundreds of dollars/month. Chroma and LanceDB are improving but still heavy for quick in-memory microservice restarts. Anyone built a lightweight embedded alternative?
problems.author: vector_dev

problems.title: ConfigMap drift detection without heavy gitops controllers
problems.body: Small dev teams running k8s without ArgoCD or Flux lack a lightweight CLI or sidecar that simply alerts when running pod environment variables drift from the repository source of truth. Existing solutions require cluster-admin operator privileges and high memory overhead.
